summary: Fourteen days of well-covered CGM data (98.7% coverage) show overall time-in-range of 86% with a coefficient of variation of 32.6%, alongside recurring severe hypoglycemia clusters (notably 2026-08-13 and 2026-08-14) and severe hyperglycemia clusters (2026-08-15 and 2026-08-18). No carbohydrate entries or meal boluses exist anywhere in the 14-day telemetry, and the user-declared meal strategy list is empty, which blocks direct validation of carb ratios and meal-related basal or bolus behavior. A profile switch to a diluted U200, flat-ISF configuration occurred mid-period (2026-08-13), and per user declaration the current aaps_profile is treated as authoritative for the full period, though this limits confidence in comparisons spanning the switch. The most actionable next step is closing the carbohydrate-logging gap and observing correction-bolus IOB timing before any profile parameter is changed.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM data is reliable (3995 entries, 98.7% coverage, ~5 min cadence, 10 gaps, largest 65 min, no duplicates or invalid entries). Zero carbohydrate entries exist for the entire period. A profile switch to a diluted U200, flat-ISF configuration occurred on 2026-08-13, roughly at the midpoint of the window. Three GLP-1 doses and one occlusion/pump-error announcement are recorded as potential confounders.

analysis_steps.findings: Aggregate glucose average 121.6 mg/dL, SD 39.7, CV 32.6%, TIR 86.0%, TAR 8.9%, TBR 5.1%. Severe lows occurred on 2026-08-13 (42-51 mg/dL), 2026-08-14 (41-48 mg/dL) and 2026-08-21 (42 mg/dL). Severe highs occurred on 2026-08-15 and 2026-08-18 (285-293 mg/dL). Several correction boluses are followed by large delayed drops at 120-360 minutes, temporally consistent with the severe-low clusters, suggesting possible insulin stacking rather than a pure basal defect. Repeated user-initiated Temporary Targets (108-135 mg/dL) indicate active self-management of known risk windows.

analysis_steps.findings: Overnight local hours 0-1 show elevated time-below-range (11.4% and 18.5%) tapering by hour 4-6, competing with an evening (18:00-22:00) correction-bolus stacking hypothesis as the driver rather than the 00:00 basal segment. A recurring afternoon rise (10:00-17:00 local) peaks at hour 16 (162.8 mg/dL average, 32.1% time above range), coinciding with the lowest daytime basal segment (0.5 U/h) and the tightest carb ratio segment (10.5 g/U), but cannot be separated from an unlogged meal given zero carbohydrate entries. Target segments (90/100/90 mg/dL) show no direct evidence of a defect.

analysis_steps.findings: A single flat ISF segment (56 mg/dL/U) coexists with wide effective sensitivity swings (roughly 27.8-178.7 mg/dL/U equivalent) driven by Dynamic ISF, making it unclear whether the flat ISF is mismatched by time of day or Dynamic ISF is functioning as designed. Five carb ratio segments exist but cannot be validated because no carbohydrate entries exist in any therapy_response_windows or treatments. DIA of 10 hours is plausible given very low total daily insulin (~19.7 U/day) and diluted U200 insulin, but may also contribute to IOB persistence implicated in the stacking hypothesis; this cannot yet be isolated from repeated close-interval correction dosing.

analysis_steps.findings: The strongest, most resolvable gap is the total absence of carbohydrate logging, which blocks conclusive interpretation of the afternoon (10:00-17:00 local, peak hour 16) hyperglycemia pattern and limits carb ratio and basal evaluation in that window. The overnight (00:00-01:00 local) hypoglycemia pattern is better explained by evening correction-bolus stacking interacting with a 10-hour DIA than by the 00:00 basal segment, based on repeated delayed-drop correction events at 120-360 minutes. Automation settings (SMB, UAM, safety limits, Dynamic ISF) show no clear internal defect; effective sensitivity variability is more likely explained by Dynamic ISF function than a flat-ISF mismatch, though this remains unresolved with current sample size. No profile or AAPS parameter change is supported by the current evidence; the safe next step is targeted observation (carb logging, correction-time IOB tracking, temp-target/SMB clarification) before any single change, made one at a time.

Early morning local hours (4-7) show strong control (95-98% time in range), suggesting fasting-period dosing is currently well matched.
The user is actively engaged in self-management, using Temporary Targets around known risk windows (activity, GLP-1 dosing) rather than relying solely on the base profile.
Coefficient of variation (32.6%) remains below common high-variability thresholds despite the presence of some severe excursions.

education: Coefficient of variation (CV) reflects overall glucose variability; values below roughly 36% are generally considered lower-risk, and the observed 32.6% sits in that range despite the presence of some severe excursions.

Dynamic ISF adjusts effective insulin sensitivity per loop cycle based on recent deviation and eventual glucose, which can produce wide apparent sensitivity swings around a single flat profile ISF value without indicating a profile defect.

Correction boluses given while earlier insulin is still active (insulin on board, or IOB) can combine with new insulin action and increase the risk of a later, delayed low if not spaced according to duration of insulin action (DIA).

Without logged carbohydrate entries, a closed-loop system cannot distinguish between an under-sized basal or carb ratio segment and an unannounced meal, which is why carbohydrate logging is often the fastest way to clarify a recurring glucose pattern.
safety_notes: This is decision-support content only; it does not constitute medical advice and does not replace guidance from a qualified care team.
Every proposed change described in this analysis must be independently verified by the user and, where relevant, discussed with a care team before being applied.
Changes to insulin-delivery settings should be made one at a time, never in combination with another dependent setting, so that the effect of each change can be observed clearly.
Glucose should be monitored closely after any change, with particular attention to the hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia patterns already identified in this analysis.
No automated or immediate change to AAPS settings is implied or should be made based on this analysis alone.
